rationale: This is a cosmetic re-specification of the already-accepted LeveredCapacityBuild (swapping the cash-flow net-debt-issuance leg for the balance-sheet identity that largely subsumes it), and since ΔLT/lagAT plus PP&E growth together approximate total asset growth, any result is likely a restatement of the Cooper-Gulen-Schill asset growth anomaly rather than a genuine funding-source interaction.

Subtracting cash acquisition outlays to isolate the paper-funded component of intangible growth is a substantive rather than cosmetic change to StockSwapIntangibleExpansion and the coverage argument is sound, though the netting is crude (aqc buys tangible assets too, and asset-scaled flows are compared to a stock difference) and the csho-growth leg on its own is the well-documented net share issuance anomaly, so the incremental content over that main effect must be demonstrated.

Both legs are standalone published anomalies — the hiring-rate/employment-growth anomaly (Bazdresch-Belo-Lin) and net share issuance (Pontiff-Woodgate, Daniel-Titman) — so the product of two non-negative ranks of known negative predictors will load negatively almost by construction, and the proposal offers no way to distinguish the claimed interaction from the sum of two rediscovered main effects.

The working-capital channel is a genuinely distinct mechanism, but the construction is internally sloppy — ΔLT already contains Δdlc so the SUMRANK double-counts short-term debt, the hypothesis invokes trade credit while the expression never touches payables, and Δinvt plus ΔLT scaled by lagged assets again collapses toward the asset-growth/inventory-growth anomalies (Thomas-Zhang).

Replacing the sparse repurchase/issuance flows with a nearly universally available leverage-change-plus-dividend funding leg is a defensible diagnosis-driven fix rather than a relabeling, but the expected positive sign sits uncomfortably with the fact that the capex/lagPPENT leg is itself a reliably negative predictor and that Δ(LT/AT) falls mechanically when assets grow, so the test needs to show the conditioning survives controls for asset growth and payout yield.

This is the only proposal that adds a genuinely new conditioning dimension — where the raised capital ended up (deployed versus hoarded, per the Palazzo cash-holdings critique) — the signed difference-of-ranks construction correctly makes the short leg high-capex spenders of new equity and the long leg high-capex cash accumulators, and the expected negative sign is consistent with the expression's natural direction; the main risk is that low-capex firms cluster near zero and dilute the middle of the sort.
